newsitem.title: MEXICO: Two years on, Mexicans unsure about their president.
newsitem.headline: Two years on, Mexicans unsure about their president.

text.p: President Ernesto Zedillo, 44, completes two years in office Sunday but his intentions -- and the likely outcome of his six-year mandate -- remain a mystery to many of his countrymen.

Foreign leaders and businessmen praise him for dragging Mexico out of economic crisis, imposing the rule of law on a notoriously corrupt society and starting to dismantle the country's 67-year-old tradition of one-party government.
But many Mexicans, who are experiencing the effects of rising crime, soaring kidnappings and the country's worst economic crisis since the 1930s, are more negative.
Fond of strong, almost imperial, leaders, they criticise Zedillo as a weak, contradictory president who has yet to prove he can deliver on promises of prosperity and full democracy.

Next year "will be the real test," said leading Mexican historian Enrique Krauze. "That's when we'll see if Zedillo understands and takes on the essential incompatibility between the Mexican political system and democracy."

Zedillo believes he will pass that test. In a recent interview with Reuters, he hailed Mexico's gradual recovery from a dire economic crisis in 1995 and recent constitutional reforms to help democracy as major steps forward.
"Despite the economic problems, we have had a country with social peace, a country where -- not without difficulties -- democracy is being strengthened", Zedillo said.

While saying they recognise Zedillo's personal honesty, they complain that he has allowed his Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) more than $120 million in government money next year for congressional elections and moan about his reluctance to prosecute PRI state governors accused of breaking the law.
That mixed picture of Zedillo shows up in other areas too.

Economists and bankers give the president credit for sticking to austere free-market policies to pull Mexico out of recession -- but next year's expected growth of four percent still won't be enough to return Mexican living standards to the levels they had reached before Zedillo took office.

Zedillo has presided over slow but successful peace negotiations with Zapatista Indian rebels in the southern state of Chiapas -- but the appearance of a new, more violent rebel group, the EPR, has taken the shine off that achievement.

Zedillo won high marks when he allowed the arrest of former President Carlos Salinas's brother Raul on murder and tax fraud charges last year -- presidential families were previously above the law -- but he has since lost points because Raul has not been convicted and no charges have been brought against Carlos.
Zedillo, said opposition political scientist Lorenzo Meyer, epitomises a "lack of will, the man who doesn't want to take on the role. He would seem to be a president by mistake."

Modest and unusually austere in his personal life for a Mexican leader, Ernesto Zedillo was indeed an accidental president. Campaign manager for PRI presidential hopeful Luis Donaldo Colosio, Zedillo became the candidate when Colosio was murdered in March 1994, five months before the elections.

Zedillo won the presidency in what was generally acclaimed as Mexico's cleanest modern election -- but four weeks later, the Mexican peso crashed and foreign investors fled, throwing the economy into its worst recession since the 1930s and ruining the Yale-educated economist's reputation.

Ever since, the president has struggled to shake off the impression that he does not enjoy his job. There are periodic rumours that he is about to resign or be pushed out, or that he has been the victim of a coup.
One of Zedillo's problems as a politician, diplomats say, is his difficulty in getting his message over to the public.

Asked by Reuters what he considered the greatest achievements of his first two years in office, Zedillo began by replying: "Well, I don't like to talk about my achievements, other people can evaluate that." Only reluctantly did he then go on to speak about some successes.
